name: Yara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Yara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do second-fix carpentry on office fit-outs in the city centre, so doors, frames, skirting, kitchen units and the wooden wall panels in meeting rooms. Right now we're on floors nine to twelve of an old insurance building, gutting it and making it look modern. I'm in at seven, I check the door schedule, and I hang maybe eight to ten doors a day if the frames are square. I like a clean finish and a quiet floor; what wears me out is the dust and the electricians standing on my sawhorses.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and how did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a fit-out firm with about forty people on the tools, and my lead hand is Dariusz, who's careful like me. I did a trade certificate after school because I liked woodwork and didn't like classrooms. I've been at this firm six years, which is a long time in fit-out, but I don't like starting over somewhere new.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a flat I own, which my grandmother left me most of the money for, so no mortgage. Fit-out pays well, and I've got over a year of costs in the bank. My brother Emre is a plumber, and we have dinner most Sundays at our mum's. I don't use any of the AI stuff; my phone is for calls and photos of the door schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. People at work keep sending each other videos of robots doing backflips, and I've never seen one hang a fire door. I'd say it once and get on with the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means nothing changes for me, which is how I like it. The office might use some program for the paperwork, but I don't touch the paperwork. My flat's paid for, my savings are good, and there's always another office floor to fit out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do, same firm, same crew. Maybe I'd finally put some savings into a second small flat to rent out, which my mum keeps telling me to do. I wouldn't learn any of the apps if nobody makes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's honestly the picture I'd pick if I could pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's always another office floor. Is there anything about your work that worries you already, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, a bit, from kneeling to fit skirting all day. And fit-out goes up and down with the office market, so two years ago we had a quiet spell where half the subcontractors got laid off. Our firm kept the full-time carpenters, but I remember how quiet the van was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the second flat, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something small near the tram line, a one-bedroom, that I could rent to a student or a nurse. I'd do the kitchen and doors myself on weekends. It's a pension for my knees, basically.

say: I'd say **I told you so** about the robot videos people share at work.
I'd point out nobody has seen a robot hang a **fire door**.
think: Nothing changes for her, which is **how she likes it**.
Her **paid-off flat** and over a year of savings make her feel secure.
do: Stay with the **same firm** and same crew, hanging doors and frames.
Think about buying a **second small flat** to rent out.
Skip the **new apps** unless the firm makes her use them.
feel: **Calm**, and openly glad this would be the outcome.
S0.quote: People at work keep sending each other videos of robots doing backflips, and I've never seen one hang a fire door.
fieldNote: She hates change and this picture asks **nothing new** of her.
Her only existing worries are her **knees** and the office fit-out cycle.
The **rental flat** idea is her version of a pension plan.

steps.text: Keep hanging doors and frames for the same fit-out firm
Buy a one-bedroom flat near the tram line to rent out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who need to worry, not us. Our estimator and the girls who do the orders might be in trouble, but software can't kneel down and scribe a skirting board to a wonky floor. I'd keep my head down at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit uneasy, because I know the firm will start pushing everything onto phones. The door schedules, the snag lists, the timesheets, all of it through an app, and I'm slow with that stuff. My hands are fine; it's the screens around the work that bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and let Dariusz handle any new app stuff on our floor, like he does now. If they force me, I'd ask Emre to sit with me on a Sunday and show me. I'd also hold off on the rental flat for a year, until I see what happens to office building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Not scared for my job, just tired already thinking about learning things I don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you hold off on the rental flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if offices change, maybe fewer companies need big offices, and then fit-out slows down. I don't know that, I'm guessing. But I'd rather sit on the money for a year than buy something and then have a quiet year at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Dariusz handle the apps. What if Dariusz leaves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be stuck, honestly, and I'd have to learn it. I'd probably be the last one on the crew to get it. I'm not proud of that, but I'm not going to pretend I'd jump at it.

say: I'd say the **office staff** should worry, not carpenters.
I'd point out software can't **scribe a skirting board** to a crooked floor.
think: Her hands-on work is safe, but the **apps around it** worry her.
She expects door schedules, **snag lists** and timesheets to move onto phones.
do: Lean on her lead hand **Dariusz** for any new app on the floor.
Ask her brother **Emre** to teach her the apps if she's forced.
Hold off on the **rental flat** for a year.
feel: **Uneasy** and already tired at the thought of learning new screens.
S1.quote: Software can't kneel down and scribe a skirting board to a wonky floor.
fieldNote: Her job looks safe to her, but **office fit-out demand** might soften, which she guesses at.
Her honest **reluctance** to learn apps is clear and she doesn't dress it up.
She relies on **trusted people**, not training courses, to adapt.

steps.text: Let lead hand Dariusz run any new snag-list app
Ask her brother Emre to teach her the timesheet app
Hold off buying the rental flat for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and the government should slow it down. At work I'd probably say we're fine for a few years because robots aren't here yet. With Emre and my mum I'd just say I don't know what to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm done at 32, if the robots really come in 2031. The office side of the firm goes in 2028, so they'll know exactly how many doors we hang and how slow I am, and then a few years later they won't need me at all. I've only ever wanted to do this one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, no rental flat, no new car, and keep every bit of the savings. I'd probably stay at the firm as long as they keep me, because moving firms feels worse than waiting. And I'd go to Emre and my mum and talk about what we'd do as a family if both of us lose our trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's gone soft under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait at the firm rather than move. Is there anything you'd learn in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I should say yes. Maybe something with people, like being a site safety officer, because people would still want a person checking robots. But I'd probably put it off until it's too late, if I'm honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most at night in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my flat is paid for but I've got forty more years of bills and no idea how I pay them. Savings last a year and a bit, then what. And Emre's in the same boat, so it's not like one of us can carry the other.

say: I'd call it **madness** and say the government should slow it down.
At work she'd claim they're **fine** for a few years until robots arrive.
think: She expects to be out of work at **32** when site robots arrive in 2031.
The firm's **office side** goes in 2028, tracking her speed before replacing her.
do: Stop **big spending**, including the rental flat and a new car.
Stay at **the firm** as long as they keep her.
Talk with her **brother and mum** about a family plan if both lose their trades.
feel: **Sick** and unsteady, like the floor has gone soft.
S2.quote: I've got forty more years of bills and no idea how I pay them.
fieldNote: Her calm public line hides a **private conviction** she'll lose her job.
She admits she'd likely **delay retraining** until too late.
Her **brother's trade** is exposed too, so family can't absorb the shock.
Strong savings help but only cover a **year and a bit** in her mind.

steps.text: Cancel the rental flat and new car, keeping all savings
Stay at the fit-out firm as long as they keep her
Plan with her brother and mum for both losing their trades

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say it should be slowed down, but I'd say it less angrily. Five years is still fast. I'd tell the crew to keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots in 2034 I'd be 35, so I've got about eight good years of doors left. That's not nothing, but it's not a career either. I'd have to change, and I hate that word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, and maybe buy the rental flat after all, because rent is something a robot can't take from me. Around year two or three I'd look at a safety officer course, if Dariusz does it with me. I'd keep the second flat simple, no big loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sick than the fast one, but it's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd hold off on the flat; now you'd buy it. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slow one I was worried about a quiet year in fit-out. Here I'm worried about not having a job at all, so having rent coming in matters more than timing it right. It's a bit backwards, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only if Dariusz does the course too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't walk into rooms full of strangers and start over well. With Dariusz there I'd actually go. Without him I'd sign up and then find reasons.

say: I'd still say it should be **slowed down**, just less angrily.
I'd tell the crew to **keep saving** because five years is still fast.
think: She has about **eight years** of door hanging left, until 35.
She knows she must **change**, which she hates.
do: Keep working and **saving** at the same firm.
Buy the **rental flat** with no big loan as a second income.
Look at a **safety officer course** in year two or three, with Dariusz.
feel: **Anxious**, but less sick than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Rent is something a robot can't take from me.
fieldNote: She **reverses** her rental flat decision and explains why, which shows real thought.
Her retraining depends on a **trusted colleague** going with her.
Eight years is enough for a plan, but her **dislike of change** keeps her worried.

steps.text: Buy a small rental flat without taking a big loan
Keep saving from the fit-out wages each month
Take a site safety officer course with Dariusz in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most predictions are wrong anyway. I'd keep working and not make a fuss. People who post about it online all day are just scaring themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd be 40, which honestly feels far away. I'd probably do this job for most of my thirties and then see. I know that's the answer of someone who doesn't want to change, but it's my answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the rental flat in the next couple of years and maybe a second one later, so by 40 I've got two rents coming in. I'd keep my job and not take any courses yet. Maybe at 35 or so I'd look at what's around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy. It's like a dentist appointment far in the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier than 35?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots on our actual floors doing doors, I'd move. Not videos, not news, real ones on our site. Until then I'd keep doing what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk about any of this with your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe with Emre, because he worries more than me. Mum would just tell me to find a husband with an office job, and that's a joke now because those go first. We'd laugh about it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and most predictions are wrong.
I'd say people **posting about it** all day are scaring themselves.
think: At **40** when robots arrive, it feels far away to her.
She admits she's answering as someone who **doesn't want to change**.
do: Buy a **rental flat** in the next couple of years and maybe a second later.
Keep the **fit-out job** with no courses for now.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a little unease like a far-off dentist visit.
S4.quote: Mum would just tell me to find a husband with an office job, and that's a joke now because those go first.
fieldNote: She will only move when she sees **real robots** on her own site.
The **rental flats** are her steady answer across the slower pictures.
Humour about **family advice** shows she isn't too shaken here.

steps.text: Buy one rental flat within two years, maybe two by 40
Keep hanging doors at the same firm without new courses
Wait until robots appear on her own site before moving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be out by 32 and I'm not someone who reinvents herself quickly. What would help is a slow, proper course where you learn with people you know, paid while you do it, not some app telling me to retrain online.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me are good at. I'm slow with new things but I'm careful, and careful people are the ones you want checking robots on a building. Somebody should be planning for that instead of just telling us to adapt.

headlineQuote: I'm slow with new things but I'm careful, and careful people are the ones you want checking robots on a building.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old second-fix carpenter** on city-centre office fit-outs, hanging doors and fitting panels.
She owns her **flat outright** and has over a year saved, but strongly dislikes change and avoids AI.
She's **calm** about AI Plateau and only mildly uneasy about Steady Disruption, mostly about apps.
AGI by 2028 leaves her **alarmed**, expecting to be out of work at 32 with no plan.
Across slower pictures she leans on **rental flats** and trusted colleagues rather than courses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be out of work by 32 and can't reinvent herself quickly.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid, in-person course** taken with people she knows, not online retraining.
